Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the first call of the quarter. Let me say how this group works, because two people here are new. We meet twice a month, on the first Monday and on the third Monday. In every call one person presents the numbers of their own market, so everybody speaks at some point in the year. You do not need a long presentation. You say what changed, you say why it changed, and you say what you do next. That is enough. Most of the people on this call work in credit, and three of us work in analytics. Nobody on this call expects perfect English. We expect you to say what you think, and we expect you to stop me when you do not follow.

I coach a lot of directors who work in a second language, and they all ask me the same question. How do I say what I do without sounding small? My answer is short. Do not translate your title. Say the work. I decide who gets credit and at what price is a better sentence than I am responsible for the credit area, because the first one tells me the work and the second one tells me a box on a chart. And then stop talking. The mistake I hear every week is the person who explains fifteen years of career before anybody asks for it. Nobody in the room is listening to the history. They are listening for one thing: what does this person decide on a Tuesday morning? Say that, in one line, and the room hears your level.

Brazil has more customers inside a digital bank than any other country outside Asia, and most of those customers never see a branch. They open the account on a phone, in about ten minutes, and nobody at the bank ever meets them. That changes the whole job of credit. A traditional bank looks the customer in the eye; a digital bank looks at data. Every payment, every late day and every change of income goes into a model, and the model decides the limit and the price. That is why these banks hire economists and not only bankers. Somebody has to write the rule that the model follows, and somebody has to answer for it when the rule is wrong.
